title: 0.1 + 0.2 on a computer
hook: Add 0.1 and 0.2 in code. Do you get exactly 0.3?

doesNotKnow: that many decimals have no finite binary form
that computers round decimals to the nearest binary fraction

misconception: A computer does decimal arithmetic exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is exactly 0.3.
objective: The learner can explain that 0.1 has no exact binary form, so a computer stores the nearest binary fraction, and these small rounding errors make 0.1 + 0.2 come out a tiny bit above 0.3.

claims.text: In binary, 0.1 is 0.000110011001100… with the block 0011 repeating forever; the 12-switch value just under 0.1, .000110011001, shows that repeat.
claims.source: Repeated doubling of the fractional part: 0.1 -> 0.2 (0) -> 0.4 (0) -> 0.8 (0) -> 1.6 (1) -> 1.2 (1) -> 0.4 (0) -> 0.8 (0) -> 1.6 (1) -> 1.2 (1) -> 0.4 ...; the remainder 0.4 recurs, so the digits 0011 repeat. Builder ran it for 20 digits: 00011001100110011001. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node doubling: 0.1 in binary = 000110011001100110011001...; 409 = 000110011001 is the under value on the number line and in the reveal; it is the true expansion truncated to 12 digits, so the 0011 repeat is visible.

claims.text: No set of the 12 switches worth 1/2 to 1/4096 adds to exactly 0.1; the two closest are 0.099853515625 (.000110011001, under by 0.000146484375) and 0.10009765625 (.000110011010, over by 0.00009765625), so the nearer one is over. The stage's number line shows both with their gaps, and the hand-built 0.099853515625 is labelled 'Close, but under. One pattern just above is closer.'
claims.source: Any sum of these switches is k/4096 for a whole number k. 0.1 x 4096 = 409.6 is not whole, so no k works. The nearest are k = 410 (0.10009765625, gap 0.00009765625) and k = 409 (0.099853515625, gap 0.000146484375). In general k/2^n can never equal 1/10, because 10 has the factor 5. | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node over all k in 0..4095: nearest 410 (0.10009765625, gap 0.00009765625), then 409 (0.099853515625, gap 0.000146484375). exact()/gapText() print those strings; message for k = 409 is 'Close, but under. One pattern just above is closer.'

claims.text: 1/3 is 0.333… in decimal and has no finite decimal form.
claims.source: Long division of 1 by 3 leaves remainder 1 at every step, so the digit 3 repeats forever; a finite decimal is k/10^n, and 3 does not divide any power of 10.

claims.text: A standard computer number (a double) keeps 53 significant binary digits and rounds to the nearest value it can store.
claims.source: IEEE 754-2019, binary64 format: precision p = 53 bits (52 stored plus an implicit leading 1); default rounding is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. JavaScript numbers are binary64 (ECMA-262, 6.1.6.1 The Number Type).

claims.text: As a double, 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055… and 0.2 as 0.2000000000000000111…: the nearest 53-digit values happen to be a hair above the decimal values (the stage labels them 'above 0.1' and 'above 0.2').
claims.source: node -e 'console.log((0.1).toPrecision(40), (0.2).toPrecision(40))' prints 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021182 and 0.2000000000000000111022302462515654042363 (builder ran it). Python: from decimal import Decimal; Decimal(0.1). | REOPENED 2026-10-14 (v3, wave D r5 revision by demo-builder): learner-visible sentence changed; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): node toPrecision(25): 0.1000000000000000055511151, 0.2000000000000000111022302; stage labels 'above 0.1', 'above 0.2'.

claims.text: 0.1 + 0.2 prints as 0.30000000000000004 in JavaScript and Python, so testing it for equality with 0.3 gives false.
Money is often counted in whole cents rather than as decimal fractions of a dollar to avoid these rounding errors.
claims.source: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002), 'Money' pattern: store amounts as integers of the smallest currency unit because floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly.

claims.text: A computer keeps the nearest value it can store, as on the number line where the nearer of the two 12-switch neighbours is the one kept ('over: nearer, kept').
claims.source: IEEE 754 (2008/2019): round-to-nearest (roundTiesToEven) is the default rounding for binary formats; section number not checked, fact-checker to confirm (same source family as c4). The 12-switch number line is an analogy computed by gapText() in Demo.tsx (409/4096 and 410/4096 against 409.6/4096). | Added 2026-10-14 (v3) by demo-builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Same source family as c4 (verified 2026-10-13): IEEE 754 default rounding for binary formats is roundTiesToEven (from my knowledge, sec. 4.3.3 in 754-2008/2019; standard not opened). Analogy check: on the stage 410/4096 is nearer than 409/4096 (0.0000977 vs 0.000146), labelled 'over: nearer, kept'.

recall.question: A program prints 0.1 + 0.7 as 0.7999999999999999. What is the best explanation?
options: A bug in the computer's adder
0.1 and 0.7 have no exact binary form, so they are stored rounded
The program deliberately cuts answers to 16 digits
recall.why: Like 1/3 in decimal, 0.1 and 0.7 repeat forever in binary. The computer stores the nearest binary fraction, and the small errors show up in the sum.
